name: Coenzyme Q10

lead: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble molecule that carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and acts as an antioxidant. The body makes it, and levels fall with age and with statin use.

It is sold as an oral supplement and is added to some anti-aging creams. Evidence for cosmetic effects is limited and mostly from small or topical studies, while its best-supported uses concern cardiovascular and mitochondrial contexts.

paras: CoQ10 shuttles electrons in oxidative phosphorylation and regenerates other antioxidants such as vitamin E. Topically it has been studied for reducing oxidative damage in skin.
Generally well tolerated, with occasional digestive upset or insomnia. It may reduce the effect of warfarin. Legal as a supplement; absorption varies with formulation.

lead: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone, ubidecarenone) is a lipid-soluble benzoquinone made by the human body and found in meat, fish, seed oils and some vegetables [1]. It is a cofactor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, where it supports ATP production, and it also acts as a membrane antioxidant [1][2]. The body synthesises it through a pathway that shares an early step with cholesterol, via HMG-CoA reductase, which is why statin drugs have been proposed to lower CoQ10 levels [1].

It is sold over the counter as an oral supplement and is used as an ingredient in some cosmetics and energy drinks, but Wikipedia notes it is not approved by the US FDA for treating any medical condition and that its manufacture is not regulated, so brands and batches may differ [1]. The best-studied uses are cardiovascular, with the Q-SYMBIO randomised trial in heart failure being a frequently cited example, alongside statin muscle symptoms, migraine, Parkinson's disease and fertility [3][4][5][6].
In appearance contexts it is promoted for skin ageing, usually topically, and in training communities it is mainly discussed with statins, heart health and mitochondrial support [7][8][9].
infobox: Dietary supplement; not FDA-approved for any condition [1]

paras: CoQ10 consists of a benzoquinone head and a tail of ten isoprene units. In its pure form it is an orange lipophilic powder, insoluble in water [1]. Ubiquinone is the name assigned by the IUPAC-IUB commission in 1975 because of its ubiquity from bacteria to humans [1]. In mitochondria it carries electrons between complexes of the respiratory chain; it is also found in other cell membranes and takes part in proton and calcium transport [1][2]. It is reduced to ubiquinol during or after intestinal absorption [1].

Primary CoQ10 deficiency arises from mutations in at least 15 biosynthesis genes and can cause serious disease, for example steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in some patients with COQ gene mutations [1][10]. Wikipedia notes that plasma measurements reflect dietary intake rather than tissue status, so clinical centres typically measure CoQ10 in fibroblasts, muscle biopsies or blood mononuclear cells [1].

CoQ10 is included in anti-ageing creams for its antioxidant role in skin. A 2024 review examined the role of CoQ10 in skin ageing and opportunities for topical intervention, and a 2021 systematic review of over-the-counter topical anti-ageing agents covers it among other ingredients [9][11]. Evidence for visible changes is mostly from small or topical studies.

CoQ10 has been studied as an adjunct in heart failure, myocardial infarction, migraine prevention, Parkinson's disease, fatigue, fertility in women with diminished ovarian reserve, kidney disease and several other conditions [3][12][4][5][13][6][14]. It is not an approved drug for these conditions.

CoQ10 is absorbed like other lipids, with bile and pancreatic enzymes forming micelles, and food, especially with fat, greatly enhances absorption. It travels in chylomicrons and lipoproteins and is excreted through bile and faeces [1]. After oral dosing the plasma peak occurs 6 to 8 hours later, sometimes with a second peak near 24 hours, and an elimination half-time of about 33 hours was found in a study using deuterium-labelled CoQ10 [1]. Because of its size and lipophilicity, bioavailability from supplements can be low, and water-soluble and cyclodextrin formulations have been developed to improve it, while nanoparticle approaches have given inconsistent results [1][15].

Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase and may reduce CoQ10 in blood, but Wikipedia states it is unclear whether they lower CoQ10 in muscle tissue and that evidence does not support supplementation improving statin side effects; a 2018 meta-analysis found preliminary evidence for reduced muscle symptoms while 2015 and 2024 analyses found no effect on statin myopathy [1].

Cardiovascular outcomes have been examined most. Wikipedia summarises that a 2014 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence on preventing heart disease, a 2016 Cochrane review found no effect on blood pressure, and a 2021 Cochrane review found no convincing evidence to support or refute use in heart failure, while a 2017 meta-analysis of heart failure patients reported 31 percent lower mortality and better exercise capacity at 30 to 100 mg per day [1]. The Q-SYMBIO trial randomised patients with moderate to severe heart failure for two years to test effects on morbidity and mortality [3].

A randomised trial published in Neurology in 2005 tested CoQ10 for migraine prophylaxis [4], and a dose-ranging trial in early Parkinson's disease reported evidence of slowing of functional decline [5]. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined fatigue [13], and a 2024 meta-analysis examined pretreatment in women with diminished ovarian reserve undergoing IVF [6]. A crossover trial tested CoQ10 and nicotinamide riboside in chronic kidney disease [14], and a trial examined effects on inflammation after myocardial infarction [12].

Registered trials include studies in male infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome, lupus in children, cyclic vomiting syndrome, geriatric bipolar depression and ageing-related symptoms [16][17][18][19][20][21].

Oral CoQ10 is generally well tolerated. Reported effects are mostly gastrointestinal, such as nausea and abdominal pain, along with rashes and headaches, and doses of 100 to 300 mg per day have been associated with insomnia or elevated liver enzymes; an observed-safe-level assessment found the evidence acceptable at intakes up to 1,200 mg per day [1]. Caution is advised in bile duct obstruction, pregnancy and breastfeeding [1].

CoQ10 may inhibit the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, probably because of structural similarity to vitamin K, and may affect theophylline, so it is not recommended for people taking warfarin [1]. A forum user asked about drug interactions before trying a CoQ10 protocol while on several heart-rhythm medicines [22].

On T Nation, CoQ10 is most often raised alongside statins, with users recommending pairing a statin with CoQ10 and a long thread about cholesterol theory describing statins as blocking CoQ10 production, which these posters said might affect the heart and muscle [7][8]. It is also mentioned in testosterone-therapy bloodwork discussions, in mitochondrial protocols, and in a longevity thread as a supplement with supposedly great benefits [23][24][22][25]. A writer notes that most cardiologists react poorly when patients mention supplements other than fish oil or CoQ10 [26]. Users also post laboratory CoQ10 results with reference ranges [27][28].

lore.intro: In training and testosterone-therapy forums CoQ10 is discussed chiefly as a companion to statins and a general heart and mitochondrial supplement [7][22][8].
